title: Unlocking the Duality between Flow and Field Matching
claim: Two seemingly different generative frameworks coincide on a natural subclass, while the broader field-based family is strictly more expressive.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, taxonomy box then three field/flow sketches
description: A four-panel horizontal figure. Panel (a) is a nested-box Venn-style taxonomy: a large green rounded box labeled IFM contains EFM, and an inner orange box containing 'CFM ≡ Forward-only IFM', Flow-Matching, Diffusion, and PFGM++. Panel (b), CFM, shows a blue source blob π_T morphing through intermediate blobs into a purple target π_0 along p_t(x), with black trajectory arrows. Panel (c) shows the same transport as field lines E(x̃) running between two light-green planes along a z axis, from blob π_L to π_0. Panel (d) shows EFM as a dipole-like field with solid and dotted lines looping around and returning, which signals reversed orientation. Orange marks CFM, green marks IFM and field objects. The eye goes first to the colored taxonomy box, then the field-line diagrams on the right.
caption: Overview of the flow–field duality. We establish that CFM and forward-only IFM induce the same data-space generative dynamics (§3): CFM ≡forward-only IFM ⊊IFM. Panel (a) summarizes the resulting taxonomy. While conventional CFM (b, §2.1) admits an equivalent forward-only field representation (c, §2.2), general IFM is strictly more expressive: it includes EFM (d, §2.2), which admits returning trajectories whose transport maps reverse orientation and therefore cannot be realized by any CFM flow (§4).
abstract: Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) unifies conventional generative paradigms such as diffusion and flow-based models. Interaction Field Matching (IFM) is a recently proposed framework that generalizes Electrostatic Field Matching (EFM), rooted in Poisson Flow Generative Models (PFGM). While both frameworks define generative dynamics, they start from different objects: CFM specifies a conditional probability path in data space, whereas IFM specifies a physics-inspired interaction field in an augmented data space. This raises a basic question: are CFM and IFM genuinely different, or are they two descriptions of the same underlying dynamics? We show that they coincide for a natural subclass of IFM, which we call forward-only IFM. Specifically, we give explicit constructions in both directions and show that CFM and forward-only IFM induce the same family of data-space dynamics. General IFM, however, is strictly more expressive: already in EFM, its sampling rule yields transport maps that reverse orientation with positive probability, something no CFM flow can do. Our findings suggest using the probabilistic and geometric views jointly when developing generative models, and exploring field-based transport beyond the forward-only regime.
